title: User management: add, modify, lock, delete
lead: Manage the lifecycle of an account safely with useradd, passwd, usermod, groupadd, chage and userdel.
objectives: You create an account with a home directory and shell using `useradd -m -s` and set its password with `passwd`.
You add users to groups with `usermod -aG` and know what happens if the `-a` is forgotten.
You lock accounts with `usermod -L` and manage password policy with `chage`.
You know the difference between `userdel` and `userdel -r` and think about preserving data before deleting.

sections.title: Creating accounts: useradd and passwd
body: When a new employee arrives you create an account for them. These actions change system files (`/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/group`), so they need **root privileges**, i.e. `sudo`.

`useradd` does **not create a home directory on every distribution by default**, so add `-m`. `-s /bin/bash` sets the login shell. The new home is filled with template files from `/etc/skel`. `passwd` sets the password; nothing is shown while you type, which is normal.
Debian/Ubuntu also have the interactive `adduser` wrapper; Rocky/Alma do not (use `useradd` there). In scripts prefer `useradd`, which works everywhere.

commands.where: When adding a new employee or service account.
commands.why: Everyone gets separate files and permissions.

commands.what: Sets or changes the account's password.
commands.why: An account without a password cannot log in.

commands.what: Manages password aging (`-d 0` forces a change at first login).
commands.where: To force a new account to change its password at first login.
commands.why: The temporary password set by the admin does not become permanent.

sections.tip: Keep account names lowercase ASCII (`alice`, `testuser`). Spaces, accented characters and capitals cause trouble.
sections.warn: Adding users on a real VM changes the system. Take a snapshot of your VM first (module 0.2). Do not type passwords on the command line (`chpasswd` leaves them in history).

sections.title: Modifying: usermod, groupadd, groups
body: `usermod` changes an existing account. Most used: `-aG group` (**append** to group), `-s` (shell), `-L` (lock), `-U` (unlock). Use `groupadd` to create a group; after a group change the user must **log in again**.
The classic mistake: `usermod -G devs alice` without `-a`. It wipes all of alice's supplementary groups and leaves only `devs`, including `wheel`. The user loses sudo rights. Always use `-aG`.
Sudo rights come from membership in `wheel` on Rocky/Alma and `sudo` on Ubuntu. Do not edit `/etc/sudoers` by hand; use `visudo`, which checks the syntax.

commands.where: When creating a shared group for a project team.
commands.why: You grant access to the group, not to each person.

commands.what: Adds the user to a group while keeping existing groups.
commands.where: When putting someone in a team or the sudo group.
commands.why: Without `-a` the old groups are removed.

commands.what: Locks the account (password login is disabled); `-U` unlocks.
commands.where: When an employee leaves or an account looks suspicious.
commands.why: Cuts access at once while data stays intact.
Confirms the lock was really applied.
Shows the membership was added and old ones were not removed.

sections.tip: After a group change an open session keeps using the old groups; the user must log out and back in.
sections.danger: `usermod -G` (without `-a`) removes all of a user's supplementary groups. On an admin account this can remove sudo access and lock you out of the system. Always write `-aG` and check with `id`.

sections.title: Deleting: userdel and the home directory
body: `userdel NAME` removes the account from `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow` and `/etc/group`, but **leaves the home directory and its files**. The directory then belongs to a UID with no owner. `userdel -r` also deletes the home directory and mail spool permanently.

The safe order in real life: (1) lock with `usermod -L`, (2) check running processes and cron jobs, (3) back up the home directory, (4) only then delete. You can find files of a deleted user with `find / -user UID`.
If the user has a session or running process, `userdel` errors out; end the session first.

commands.what: Deletes the account, keeps the home directory.
commands.where: After the employee left and data was backed up.
commands.why: Closes the account without risk of data loss.

commands.what: Deletes account, home directory and mail spool permanently.
commands.where: Only when the data is truly not needed.
commands.why: Cleans up disk space and leftovers.

commands.what: Shows the home directory still exists.
commands.why: You see that leftover directories remain ownerless.

sections.warn: `userdel -r` cannot be undone: photos, documents and keys are gone. Back up first, snapshot your VM, lock the account, and re-read the user name before pressing ENTER.
sections.danger: With `sudo rm -r /home/NAME`, a wrong path (a stray space or missing name) deletes other data. Run it only for the `testuser` you created and type the full path.

t01.text: Try your sudo rights with `sudo whoami`. The output must be `root`.
t01.hint: `student` is in the wheel group, so sudo works.

t02.text: Show alice's account record with `grep alice /etc/passwd`.

t03.text: List which users have a home directory with `ls /home`.

t04.text: Read the password hashes with `sudo cat /etc/shadow`. The file is root-only.

t05.text: See the permissions and owner of alice's home directory with `sudo ls -ld /home/alice`.
t05.hint: `-d` lists the directory itself, not its content.

t07.text: Find the members of the `devs` group with `grep devs /etc/group`.

t08.text: List alice's home content (including hidden files) with `sudo ls -la /home/alice`.
t08.hint: Reading another user's home needs root.

t09.text: Predict: what does `cat /etc/shadow` do as a normal user? Run it and verify.

t10.text: Predict: how do the permissions of alice's home directory look? Guess first, then verify with `sudo ls -ld /home/alice`.

t11.text: Predict: what does `id carol` return for an account that does not exist yet? Run it.

t12.text: Debug: the `userdel -r alice` in `~/offboard.sh` deletes the home directory that must be kept for the audit. Rewrite the script so it contains `sudo userdel alice` without `-r`.

t13.text: Mini project: write a three-line plan into `~/new_user_plan.txt`: `sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash carol`, `sudo passwd carol` and `sudo usermod -aG devs carol`.
t13.hint: Use `>` on the first line and `>>` on the rest.

t14.text: Challenge: the script `~/onboard.sh` must create `dave` with `-m -s /bin/bash -G devs`, then force a password change at first login with `chage -d 0 dave`. Make the script `chmod 750`.

t15.text: TICKET #4210: `eve` has left the company. First lock the account, then delete it (keeping the home directory). Write the commands in order into `~/offboard_eve.txt`.
t15.hint: `sudo usermod -L eve` and `sudo userdel eve`; do not use `-r`.

t16.text: TICKET #4211: `frank` will become an administrator on the server (Rocky/Alma). Write the command into `~/frank.txt`.
t16.hint: `sudo usermod -aG wheel frank`; do not forget `-a`.

vm.intro: This section changes the system. Take a snapshot of your VM first. Work only on `testuser` and `labteam` from this section; do not touch your own account.

v01.title: Create an account
v01.text: Create the `testuser` account with a home directory and bash shell and paste its record.

blocks.cmd:
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash testuser
getent passwd testuser

differs: If you see `user already exists` the account was created earlier; `getent passwd testuser` is enough.
On Ubuntu the UID may be a number other than 1001.

v02.title: Set a password
v02.text: Set a password for `testuser`. Nothing is shown while typing. Paste the success message.
differs: On Rocky/Alma the message is `passwd: all authentication tokens updated successfully.`
A too short/simple password triggers a warning but is still accepted (as root).

v03.title: Add to a group
v03.text: Create the `labteam` group, add `testuser` with **-aG** and paste the `id` output.

blocks.cmd:
sudo groupadd labteam
sudo usermod -aG labteam testuser
id testuser

differs: If the group exists you get `groupadd: group 'labteam' already exists`; continue.
If `labteam` is missing next to the primary group, check the letters `-a` and `-G`.

v04.title: Lock the account

blocks.cmd:
sudo usermod -L testuser
sudo passwd -S testuser

differs: On Rocky/Alma the status is shown as `LK`.

v05.title: Password policy
v05.text: Paste the `chage -l` output; force a password change at first login.

blocks.cmd:
sudo chage -d 0 testuser
sudo chage -l testuser
blocks.expected:
Last password change                : password must be changed
Password expires                    : never
...

differs: The output must contain the `Last password change` line; the value may be `password must be changed` or a date.
If `chage: command not found`, the `shadow-utils` (Rocky) or `passwd` (Ubuntu) package is missing.

v06.title: userdel keeps the home
v06.text: Delete the account WITHOUT `-r`; then show that the account is gone but its home directory remains.

blocks.cmd:
sudo userdel testuser
getent passwd testuser
ls -ld /home/testuser

differs: `getent` prints nothing; the account is deleted.
The home directory's owner now shows as a number (1001) instead of a name; that means an ownerless directory.
On `user is currently used by process`, end the user's session.

v07.title: Cleanup
v07.text: Clean up the now unneeded test directory and group. Type the full path in the commands. Press "Done" when finished.

blocks.cmd:
sudo rm -r /home/testuser
sudo groupdel labteam
ls /home

differs: `groupdel: group 'labteam' does not exist` means it is already gone.
If you notice you mistyped the path, do not press ENTER; be sure of the full path `/home/testuser`.

q1.q: What does `sudo usermod -G devs alice` (without `-a`) do?
options: Adds alice to devs and keeps the others
Removes all of alice's supplementary groups and leaves only devs
q1.explain: -G replaces the supplementary group list; without `-a` (append) old groups such as wheel are lost.

options: The home directory is deleted too
The account is deleted but the home directory stays
q2.explain: The records are removed; `/home/alice` and its files stay on disk. Deleting them needs `-r`.

q3.q: How do you cut an account's access immediately without deleting it?
q3.explain: `usermod -L` disables password login; the account and data stay and `-U` brings it back.

q4.q: Membership in which group gives sudo rights on Rocky/Alma?
q4.explain: On the RHEL family the sudo group is `wheel`; on Debian/Ubuntu it is `sudo`.

summary: `sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash NAME` creates an account; `passwd` sets a password; `chage -d 0` forces a change at first login.
When adding to a group always use `usermod -aG`; forgetting `-a` removes the old groups.
`usermod -L` locks, `-U` unlocks; locking is the safe first step before deleting.
`userdel` keeps the home directory, `userdel -r` deletes it permanently; back up and snapshot first.

glossary.meaning: The administrator group that grants sudo on the RHEL family (`sudo` on Debian).
Template files copied into a new home directory.
An account whose password login is disabled (`usermod -L`).
A directory that still belongs to the UID of a deleted user.
A restorable point-in-time image of a VM.
